players.product: solid-oxide fuel cells for data-center onsite power

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 and full-year 2025 results (acting principal financial officer Maciej Kurzymski, non-GAAP): Q4 revenue $777.7 million, up 35.9% year over year; Q4 gross margin 31.9% (the call compares it with 39.3% in 2024); Q4 operating income $133 million vs $133.4 million a year earlier; Q4 adjusted EBITDA $146.1 million; Q4 EPS 45 cents vs 43 cents. Full year: record revenue of $2 billion, up 37.3% from 2024; non-GAAP gross margin 30.3% (vs 28.7%); non-GAAP operating profit $221 million, up $113.4 million; adjusted EBITDA $271.6 million; free cash flow positive for the second year in a row. CEO KR Sridhar: record revenue, gross margin and operating margin for the year, and 'Bloom is rapidly becoming the standard for on-site power.'
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 revenue $777.7 million, up 35.9%; FY2025 revenue $2 billion, up 37.3%; FY non-GAAP operating profit $221 million; FY adjusted EBITDA $271.6 million

quarterly_data.signal: Backlog: 'Our product backlog increased 140% year over year to about $6 billion' (Kurzymski: it 'has more than doubled from a year ago'), plus around $14 billion of service backlog; the product backlog is 100% attached to service. Commercial and industrial (C&I) backlog grew over 135% year over year across telecom, manufacturing, logistics, retail, healthcare and education. Management says demand from data-center and C&I customers is 'secular and growing' ('Bring your own power has become the mantra for data centers and power-hungry factories') and that the backlog has a healthy customer mix and does 'not have oversized concentration to any one customer.' Bloom will invest further in its commercial team in 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: product backlog about $6 billion (up 140%); around $14 billion service backlog; C&I backlog up over 135%

quarterly_data.signal: Customer mix: the reported backlog 'includes half a dozen hyperscale and neo cloud end customers, compared to just one a year ago', and Bloom uses a master contract structure so these customers can come back with repeat orders. Over two-thirds of the C&I business year over year comes from repeat customers. Geography: two years ago over 80% of the US backlog was in California and the Northeast (high power-cost states); this year over 80% comes from other, lower-cost states with robust natural-gas infrastructure and policy that supports on-site power, where Bloom says it is cost competitive. Bloom does not break out US vs international backlog. The US remains the key focus for the foreseeable future; international lags because gas/LNG for new projects is scarce, e.g. in Europe.
quarterly_data.figure: half a dozen hyperscale and neo cloud end customers in backlog (vs just one a year ago); over 80% of US backlog outside California and the Northeast; over two-thirds of C&I business from repeat customers

quarterly_data.signal: Initial FY2026 guidance ('we expect 2026 to accelerate'): revenue $3.1 billion to $3.3 billion, non-GAAP gross margin approximately 32%, capital spending $150 million to $200 million and cash flow from operations close to $200 million. The transcript prints the non-GAAP operating income guide as 'approximately $125 million to $475 million' (quoted as printed; the range looks garbled). Bloom will keep investing in R&D and commercial efforts. Asked about bullish long-range comments on Bloom from a supplier (the analyst named it as MTAR Technologies), KR said 'we have not provided any long-term guidance' and that 'the horizon at best is six months' as the digital-infrastructure buildout accelerates.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 guide: revenue $3.1 billion to $3.3 billion; non-GAAP gross margin approximately 32%; capex $150 million to $200 million; operating cash flow close to $200 million

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity: Bloom signaled last year that it is going from one to two gigawatts, and 'going forward, we'll just continuously keep expanding our capacity' as a quarter-by-quarter decision. 'We have standing orders with our suppliers of equipment, with our supply chain, with everybody else to ramp up as quickly as we need to'; 'Our return on invested capital for capacity expansion is a few months, not years.' KR says Bloom can scale 'without facing the multiyear delivery backlogs plaguing traditional suppliers' and promises customers 'Bloom will not be the bottleneck to your growth.' Speed proof point: it delivered 'a hyperscale AI factory order in fifty-five days against a ninety-day commitment.' Book-and-ship was 'a significant double-digit percentage' of 2025 business and is expected to stay in double digits.
quarterly_data.figure: capacity going from one to two gigawatts; hyperscale AI factory order delivered in fifty-five days vs a ninety-day commitment; book-and-ship a significant double-digit percentage of 2025

quarterly_data.signal: 800V DC transition: KR says AI racks will need 800 volts DC ('This switch to 800 volts DC is a necessity and not a choice') because upcoming AI racks will consume almost 100 times more power than traditional CPU racks. Grid, turbine or engine-powered sites will need transformers, rectifiers and power-conditioning gear to convert high-voltage AC, while 'Bloom, and only Bloom, natively produces 800 volts DC today.' 'Starting now, every Bloom server we ship will be 800 volts DC ready', with a removable adapter for legacy AC environments, and Bloom offers to convert previously shipped servers with simple modifications. KR says it also cuts copper use (copper is short in transformers) and efficiency losses.
quarterly_data.figure: every Bloom server shipped from now is 800 volts DC ready; AI racks almost 100 times the power of traditional CPU racks

quarterly_data.signal: New platform 'apps' for AI data centers: (1) rapid load following of the AI load 'without requiring batteries', running islanded without backup generators; KR says this removes the battery supply-chain constraint. (2) Combined cooling: high-quality heat from on-site fuel cells drives absorption chillers that deliver chilled water at around five degrees Celsius. 'We think we can reduce electricity usage in the data center by at least 20%.' Bloom already runs this mode to cool its own factory as a customer demo. KR says the approach avoids hydrofluorocarbons and the vapor-compression chiller supply chain.
quarterly_data.figure: absorption chilling could cut data-center electricity use by at least 20%

quarterly_data.signal: Service business: profitable for eight quarters in a row, with Q4 2025 service gross margin of 20% (Kurzymski: approximately 20% non-GAAP, a first). Full-year service non-GAAP gross profit was $29.7 million, and Q4 product margins were 37%. Every order carries a 100% service attach rate. Bloom has 'a few trillion cell hours of field operation', and 'More than 6 billion data points come from our field' every day to feed a digital twin of every fuel-cell stack, used to extend life and cut service cost. Kurzymski expects annual service improvement, with some quarterly volatility.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 service gross margin 20%; FY2025 service non-GAAP gross profit $29.7 million; Q4 product margins 37%

quarterly_data.signal: Supply chain and balance sheet: year-end inventory was $643 million, slightly above plan, held on purpose as Bloom prepares for a strong 2026 ('we are not pinching the last penny on the amount of inventory we hold'). Total cash was $2.5 billion after the convertible bond raise; Q4 operating cash flow was $113.9 million and Q4 CapEx $57 million. Bloom works with supply-chain partners on scale and process efficiencies; 'double-digit cost reduction is in our DNA every single year'; KR says these cost cuts let Bloom neutralize much of a tariff-driven cost rise and, during COVID, absorb higher logistics costs without raising prices. KR describes a diversified, global supply chain combined with in-house production.
quarterly_data.figure: year-end inventory $643 million; total cash $2.5 billion; Q4 operating cash flow $113.9 million; Q4 CapEx $57 million

quarterly_data.signal: Competitive position and pricing: Bloom now competes in the same class as combined-cycle gas turbines ('We have hundreds of megawatts going into the gigawatts' at single sites). It is winning even in states where electricity is traditionally cheap, and KR cites load following, modular growth and native DC as advantages over turbines. On pricing: 'we don't see us having to choose between growth and profitability', while legacy turbine and engine suppliers are raising prices. As demand context, KR cited the latest hyperscaler capex increases (Amazon, Google): 'On-site power is a necessity.' No M&A needed beyond selective platform deals.

connects_to.relationship: fuel-cell power for AI data centers
